sources.title: Grammatical and lexical sources of allomorphy in Amuzgo inflectional tone
sources.author: Yuni Kim

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Catalog Amuzgo tables; catalog grouping/variant definitions
claimBlocks.text: INALI groups Amuzgo within the Oto-Manguean family and distinguishes northern, southern, lower eastern and upper eastern variants. Its locality tables associate the eastern variants with Santa María Ipalapa and San Pedro Amuzgos in Oaxaca, while the northern and southern variants are listed in Guerrero. Self-designations vary, including nomndaa, nundá’, jñunnda and ñonndaa. These are linguistic classifications with local identities, not four separate peoples or governments; INALI recommends treating variants as languages in education and public services.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A speaker’s dictionary and writing choices
claimBlocks.text: Moisés Zeferino de Jesús García presents his dictionary as a study of his own language, developed through reflection and consultation with other speakers, teachers and scholars. He identifies Xochistlahuaca as its variety and offers it to bilingual schools, students and other learners. His introduction explains why tone and syllable distinctions matter to his spelling choices, while acknowledging that vocabulary remains incomplete. This is a particular author’s 2012 documentation project, rather than a universal Amuzgo orthographic rule.

The 2018 Ñomndaa curriculum names educators from communities including Xochistlahuaca, Huehuetónoc, Tlacoachistlahuaca and Cozoyoapan among its authors. Its diagnostic consultation asked teachers, students and parents about language use and learning priorities. The program reports family interest in reading and writing Ñomndaa alongside Spanish, and recommends producing materials for particular variants with students, teachers and parents. These are the curriculum’s documented priorities and recommendations, rather than proof of present implementation in every school.

Yuni Kim’s San Pedro Amuzgos study shows that tone helps express grammatical relationships, including who participates in an action. Much of its evidence comes from native-speaker linguist Fermín Tapia García’s extensive verb manuscript, part of which Kim checked with him during visits in 2012 and 2013. The article proposes an explanation for differences between ordinary verb inflection and causative forms. It also emphasizes differences among Amuzgo varieties, so its analysis should not be applied unchanged throughout Guerrero and Oaxaca.

inspections.actualMaterial: Complete INALI HTML Amuzgo variant/locality table and grouping table, plus catalog introduction and category definitions, all directly opened.
findings: Northern table explicitly lists Tlacoachistlahuaca and Xochistlahuaca, Guerrero; southern table lists Azoyú, Cuajinicuilapa and Ometepec localities in Guerrero.
Lower eastern explicitly lists Santa María Ipalapa localities; upper eastern explicitly lists San Pedro Amuzgos localities in Oaxaca.

Definition of agrupación relates a set of variants to a historically named people. Definition of variante includes structural/lexical differences and sociolinguistic identity; public-service recommendation is attributed to INALI.
inspections.limits: No current census, all-present-residence extent, exact territorial boundary, mutual-intelligibility guarantee, or separate-government inference. Undated HTML introduction still describes anticipated DOF publication; do not call that HTML a newly published 2026 policy. Dictionary imprint independently identifies the underlying catalog’s DOF publication as 14 January 2008, but no new date is assigned to the HTML.
inspections.countDecision: One catalog collection, not three works for its linked pages. Existing SIC p13-s1 substantially repackages the same four-variant data; replace/upgrade rather than inflate the substantive count.

inspections.actualMaterial: Actual 36,390,141-byte,226-page public INALI PDF downloaded over normal HTTPS. pypdf selected opening pages read; rendered PDF pp.6–7 visually confirms title, author, 2012 first-edition imprint and ISBN.
findings: Printed pp.11–12 acknowledge Fermín Tapia García as Amuzgo from San Pedro Amuzgos, Thomas Cedric Smith Stark, Esther Herrera Zendejas, Eliuth de Jesús Apóstol and Remedios Socorro Polanco Castañeda; distinguish their contributions, not claim coauthorship.
Printed pp.13–15 give the author’s own-language perspective, purposes, intended users, collection beginning2004, and selection of Xochistlahuaca.
Printed pp.15–17 explain alphabetical ordering and the author’s orthographic departures, including tone marking and controlled/ballistic syllables. Not reproduced as a lesson or universal standard.
inspections.limits: pypdf loses some accented/underlined title letters; the title and imprint were visually checked, and the Spanish subtitle is unambiguous. No first-dictionary-ever assertion: the author himself credits Tapia García’s earlier Oaxaca work. No use of his dated95% claim or vitality assessment as current population evidence. No whole dictionary reading claim.

integrationNotes: Use at most four counted works from this packet. Renew/replace the baseline p13-s1 with the primary catalog; do not give the derived SIC variant summary a second count for the same evidence.
Every counted work has its own60–85-word claim block. If root merges these into longer sections, recalculate annotation+scope+all cited body words per work against200.
Bodies are attributed explanations. Do not turn an author’s spelling argument or a2018curricular recommendation into a universal/current community mandate.
Do not copy privateEvidence fields into public cards or serve the downloaded full texts/rendered pages as Site assets. Link original public HTTPS sources.
coverageGaps: Current community-preferred spelling across localities, classroom implementation and current learner/speaker distributions were not established.
SantaMaríaIpalapa and southern-variety community-authored perspectives remain underrepresented; linguistic catalog entries are not substitutes for those voices.
The community's own interpretation of names should be expanded with explicitly attributed first-person sources rather than adopting competing external etymologies as universal fact.
